ssml: AI agents are getting good. <break time="200ms"/> Good enough to read the news, size a bet, and move real money. <break time="500ms"/> But here's the catch. <break time="300ms"/> An agent with the authority to spend is one poisoned headline away from a drained wallet.
This is Auspex. <break time="300ms"/> A prediction market where AI does all of the reading, <break time="200ms"/> and none of the deciding.

Three AI agents do the work. One drafts market questions from confirmed news. One researches each market and proposes bets. One proposes how a market resolved. <break time="400ms"/> But not one of them can create a market, bet over its limit, or resolve anything. <break time="200ms"/> Those decisions belong to a person, and to a smart contract on <sub alias="M S T">MST</sub> Blockchain.

Here's the flow. <break time="200ms"/> News arrives as untrusted text, and a story needs two independent publishers before anything happens. The proposer agent drafts a market, but a draft is only a suggestion. Strict schema validation throws out anything malformed. <break time="200ms"/> Then a human reads it as a checklist, <break time="150ms"/> and signs.

That's the review queue. The source text is fenced off as untrusted, right on the page. And the key that signs for a market lives only in a browser wallet. No server has ever seen it. <break time="200ms"/> Nine markets on chain were created exactly this way.

And because news is untrusted, it's treated like an attack. Here's a hostile headline trying to break out of its delimiters. It's flagged, and the closing tag it tried to smuggle in is redacted from the message the model receives.

Members get their own agents. Each one proposes a side, a confidence, and a stake. <break time="200ms"/> A deterministic policy gate, with no model and no network, checks that against eight rules in order, clamps the stake, and writes down a reason every time it says no.

So there are four layers that can say no. <break time="250ms"/> The schema. <break time="250ms"/> The policy gate. <break time="250ms"/> A human. <break time="400ms"/> And the chain. <break time="350ms"/> That last one matters most, because it doesn't care what the application believes.

So let's test it. <break time="200ms"/> This button on the trust page needs no wallet. It reads a real agent's on-chain cap, adds exactly one <sub alias="way">wei</sub>, and has the server sign the bet with the policy gate deliberately bypassed, which is exactly what a compromised server would do. <break time="300ms"/> Here's one a visitor ran from the live site.

The cap: <break time="150ms"/> zero point zero two <sub alias="test M S T C">tMSTC</sub>. <break time="200ms"/> The bet: <break time="150ms"/> one <sub alias="way">wei</sub> more. <break time="500ms"/> Reverted. <break time="300ms"/> Agent per T X cap exceeded, with both numbers in the error, decoded against verified source on <sub alias="M S T Scan">MSTScan</sub>. <break time="300ms"/> The app didn't stop that agent. The contract did.
And when no market is open, the button won't run at all, and it tells you why. A late bet would be refused for the wrong reason, and that would prove the wrong thing.

Authority is checked the same way. This role matrix is read live from the contract. The agent wallets hold no role at all. They can't create a market or resolve one, and winnings are paid to the owner, so a stolen agent key can't steal a thing.

Resolution follows the same rules. The resolution agent doesn't pick its own sources, and it must quote its evidence word for word. A paraphrase fails. <break time="200ms"/> A human signs the outcome, a challenge window opens, and after that, anyone can finalize, and winners claim.
Market eight, a labelled test market driven from a laptop, shows the whole lifecycle on chain, <break time="150ms"/> including every step the contract refused.
Every decision, approved or refused, lands in an append-only log with its reason. The refusals are never deleted. <break time="200ms"/> They're the evidence.

Auspex. <break time="300ms"/> AI proposes. <break time="200ms"/> Humans and the chain decide. <break time="600ms"/> It's live on <sub alias="M S T">MST</sub> testnet. The contract source is verified, and every hash in this video resolves on the explorer. <break time="400ms"/> So don't trust me. <break time="200ms"/> Check it.
